title: The Four Basic Forces
lead: Only four basic forces act in nature, and each is carried by a particle exchanged between the particles that feel it. This section sets out the strengths and ranges of the four forces and their carriers, introduces the Feynman diagram that graphs such an exchange, and relates the range of a force to the mass of the particle that carries it.
objectives: Explain the Feynman diagram for the exchange of a virtual photon between two positive charges.
Describe the Feynman diagram for the exchange of a between a proton and a neutron.
summary_html:
• The four basic forces and their carrier particles are summarized in the Table 33.1.
  • Feynman diagrams are graphs of time versus position and are highly useful pictorial representations of particle processes.
  • The theory of electromagnetism on the particle scale is called quantum electrodynamics (QED).
notes: The fourth learning objective is carried as the book prints it, with the symbol of the pion, π⁺, missing after “exchange of a”.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s own key. The unkeyed problem on the ratios of the strong force to the weak and electromagnetic forces under normal circumstances is left out. Four AP items are unkeyed and carry AI-marked suggested approaches: why gravity alone describes the Earth’s orbit, gravity against the weak force between quarks, the magnetic field of the charged Moon’s orbit, and the repulsion and the neutrons of heavy nuclei. The module prints no Check Your Understanding box, so nothing is set inline.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 33.4) The first image shows the exchange of a virtual photon transmitting the electromagnetic force between charges, just as virtual pion exchange carries the strong nuclear force between nucleons. The second image shows that the photon cannot be directly observed in its passage, because this would disrupt it and alter the force. In this case it does not get to the other charge. (Figure 33.5) The Feynman diagram for the exchange of a virtual photon between two positive charges illustrates how the electromagnetic force is transmitted on a quantum mechanical scale. Time is graphed vertically while the distance is graphed horizontally. The two positive charges are seen to be repelled by the photon exchange. (Figure 33.6) The image shows a Feynman diagram for the exchange of a π⁺ between a proton and a neutron, carrying the strong nuclear force between them. This diagram represents the situation shown more pictorially in Figure 33.4.

exercises.prompt: Two intact (not ionized) hydrogen atoms are 10 cm apart. Which of the following are true?

options: Gravity, though very weak, is acting between them.
The neutral charge means the electromagnetic force between them can be ignored.
The range is too long for the strong force to be involved.
answer.hint: Read each statement against the strength, range and sign of each force in Table 33.1.

exercises.prompt: Explain why we only need to concern ourselves with gravitational force to describe the orbit of the Earth around the Sun.

answer.solution: Go through the four forces of Table 33.1. The strong and weak forces have ranges below $10^{-15}\;\text{m}$, so they act only inside nuclei and nothing of them reaches across the distance between the Earth and the Sun. The electromagnetic force has an infinite range, but the Earth and the Sun are electrically neutral overall, so the attractions and repulsions of their charges cancel. Gravity is the weakest force, but its range is infinite and it is attractive only, so the contributions of every particle in two such enormous masses add up instead of cancelling.

exercises.prompt: Consider four forces: the gravitational force between the Earth and the Sun; the electrostatic force between the Earth and the Sun; the gravitational force between the proton and electron in a hydrogen atom, and the electrostatic force between the proton and electron in a hydrogen atom. What is the proper ordering of the magnitude of these forces, from greatest to least?

options: gravity, Earth-Sun; electrostatic, Earth-Sun; gravity, hydrogen; electrostatic, hydrogen
electrostatic, Earth-Sun; gravity, Earth-Sun; electrostatic, hydrogen; gravity, hydrogen
gravity, Earth-Sun; gravity, hydrogen; electrostatic, hydrogen; electrostatic, Earth-Sun
gravity, Earth-Sun; electrostatic, hydrogen; gravity, hydrogen; electrostatic, Earth-Sun
answer.hint: Treat the Earth and the Sun as neutral, and compare the electrostatic and gravitational forces in hydrogen with the relative strengths in Table 33.1.

exercises.prompt: Deep within a nucleon, which is the stronger force between two quarks, gravity or the weak force? Why do you think so?

answer.solution: Compare the relative strengths in Table 33.1: the weak force is about $10^{-13}$ of the strong force and gravity about $10^{-38}$, so the weak force is some $10^{25}$ times stronger than gravity. Its short range, less than $10^{-18}\;\text{m}$, is no handicap deep within a nucleon, where the quarks are close enough together for it to act, while the tiny masses of the quarks make gravity between them negligible. The weak force is the stronger.

exercises.prompt: Consider the Earth-Moon system. If we were to place equal charges on the Earth and the Moon, how large would they need to be for the electrostatic repulsion to counteract the gravitational attraction?

answer.hint: Set $kq^{2}/r^{2}$ equal to $GMm/r^{2}$; the distance cancels, so $q=\sqrt{GMm/k}$.

exercises.prompt: What is the strength of the magnetic field created by the orbiting Moon, at the center of the orbit, in the system in the previous problem? (Treat the charge going around in orbit as a current loop.) How does this compare with the strength of the Earth’s intrinsic magnetic field?

answer.solution: The charge found in the previous problem goes once around the orbit in one orbital period of the Moon, about 27.3 days, so the current of the loop is that charge divided by the period in seconds. The field at the center of a current loop is $B=\mu_{0}I/2R$, with $R$ the radius of the Moon’s orbit, about $3.84\times 10^{8}\;\text{m}$. Compare the result with the Earth’s own field at its surface, about $5\times 10^{-5}\;\text{T}$: with so small a current spread around so large a loop, the field at the center comes out many orders of magnitude weaker.

exercises.prompt: An atomic nucleus consists of positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, so the electrostatic repulsion should destroy it by making the protons fly apart. This doesn’t happen because:

options: The strong force is ~100 times stronger than electromagnetism.
The weak force generates massive particles that hold it together.
answer.hint: Compare the relative strengths of the strong and electromagnetic forces in Table 33.1.

exercises.prompt: The atomic number of an atom is the number of protons in that atom’s nucleus. Make a prediction as to what happens to electromagnetic repulsion as the atomic number gets larger. Then, make a further prediction about what this implies about the number of neutrons in heavy nuclei.

answer.solution: The electromagnetic force has an infinite range, so every proton in a nucleus repels every other one; the number of repelling pairs grows roughly as the square of the atomic number, and the total repulsion grows faster than the number of protons. The strong force has a range of about $10^{-15}\;\text{m}$, so each nucleon attracts only its nearest neighbors, and that attraction grows only in proportion to the number of nucleons. Neutrons add strong attraction without adding any repulsion, so a heavy nucleus needs proportionally more of them to hold together: heavy nuclei should have more neutrons than protons, and the excess should grow with the atomic number.

exercises.prompt: (a) Find the ratio of the strengths of the weak and electromagnetic forces under ordinary circumstances. (b) What does that ratio become under circumstances in which the forces are unified?

parts.hint: Divide the weak force’s relative strength in Table 33.1 by the electromagnetic force’s.
